newsitem.title: australia: Australian debt bought up on wages, now for CPI.
newsitem.headline: Australian debt bought up on wages, now for CPI.

text.p: *Short Australian bond and bill futures ended sharply higher in the aftermath of the AIRC granting a A$10 per week pay award, and ahead of an expected benign March quarter CPI on Wednesday.

"A$10 per week was certainly a number the market was looking for. It takes away one of the medium term threats on the inflation outlook," said Andrew Pease, senior economist at Nomura Research Australia.

"There certainly is a probability that there will be another interest rate cut. But my guess is that interest rates will stay at 6.0 percent, and today's decision means that they will stay there longer than they would have done," he added.
However, there is speculation that if the inflation report comes in weak, and given the recent patchy data flow, the Reserve Bank now has scope to cut policy if it sees the need.

Forecasts centre on a headline CPI rise of just 0.1 percent for the March quarter, bringing the annual inflation rate to 1.2 percent, while the policy-sensitive underlying rate is seen up 0.4 percent for year-on-year growth of 2.1 percent, according to a Reuters survey of economists.
One economist is predicting a underlying rate rise of just 0.2 percent, which would bring the annual rate to below 2.0 percent and under the Reserve Bank's 2.0-3.0 percent target.
However, today's AIRC decision is a more forward looking outcome, and means that wage inflation is also going to be contained within the RBA's 4.0 to 4.5 percent comfort zone.

The A$10 per week pay award compares with the Australian Council of Trade Unions claim for A$20 per week increases over the next three years and a 8.75 percent minimum rate adjustment. The government had wanted an increase of A$8 per week.
In making its decision, the Commission said that if it had granted the ACTU's claim it would have increased wage inflation to 6.0 percent per year and endangered the RBA's inflation goal.
The RBA had warned on previous occasions that it would take appropriate monetary policy action if the union claim had been awarded in full.

The market put in a strong outperformance against the dollar bloc following the wage decision, wiping out Monday's widening bias, and taking the Australian/U.S. 10-year bond yield spread close to last week's lows. More notable was the contraction at the short-end across the dollar currencies.
